attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Narada; actual author unknown
period: Date uncertain; many scholars place it in the early or middle second millennium CE, after the Bhagavata Purana
summary: A short set of aphorisms (about 84) defining bhakti as supreme love for God and describing its signs and means.
whyRead: It is the most accessible systematic account of devotion. In a few pages it defines bhakti, compares it with knowledge and action, and gives practical counsel.
questions: What is bhakti, and how is it different from ordinary love?
Is devotion a means or an end?

keyTeachings.title: Bhakti as supreme love
keyTeachings.text: The opening sutras define devotion as supreme love (parama-prema) for God, and describe it as the nature of immortality and fulfilment.

keyTeachings.title: Devotion as its own end
keyTeachings.text: The text holds that bhakti is itself the fruit, not merely a means to something else, and ranks it above action, knowledge and yoga.

keyTeachings.title: The gopis as exemplars
keyTeachings.text: The cowherd women of Vraja are named as models of devotion, since their love was total and self-forgetful.

keyTeachings.title: Means: company and self-giving
keyTeachings.text: It recommends the company of the devout, giving up sense-attachment and bad company, and offering all actions to God.

passages.about: Bhakti defined as supreme love for God
